ME M O R A N D U M 
TO:   Allison Hastey, Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment 
FROM:   Susan Morrisey, Abigail Kesner, Allison Nipert, SE2 
RE:  Key findings for Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual and Transgender (LGBT) audiences 
DATE:   January 28, 2014  
 
In order to continue developing materials for targeted audiences, we have created a summary of our 
research into Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual and Transgender (LGBT) audiences. In understanding how to 
communicate with LGBT audiences we reviewed national research into trends, messages and 
communications strategies. We also conducted primary research in the form of two focus groups: one 
with LGBT adults and one with LGBT youth in El Paso County. While the focus groups help to provide 
some insights, the findings cannot be seen as reflective of an overall trend. All this research provides the 
background for the information listed below. Below we outline preliminary recommendations on 
messages and overall direction, and suggestions to customize existing campaigns or develop new 
campaigns for LGBT audiences.  
Purpose & Methodology 
The discovery phase of our project included a review of existing research related to tobacco use, 
cessation strategies, messages and communications tactics for tobacco cessation among LGBT 
audiences. For a separate project, we also conducted two focus groups with LGBT youth and adults in El 
Paso County. The limited findings from that primary research are also included in this memo. 
Key Findings:  Research on Key Audiences 
LGBT communities have one of highest smoking rates of all disproportionately affected populations.1 
Researchers nationwide have conducted studies to determine contributing factors to this trend and 
effective messages and tactics for addressing this issue. These studies consistently show that LGBT 
populations respond better to messages targeted specifically to them. The findings from the two focus 
groups with LGBT youth and adults in El Paso County support this finding. 
                                                           
1 Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment: Tobacco Program Tobacco Prevention and Cessation for LGBT 
Communities 

--- PAGE 2 ---
2 
 
This is significantly different than the findings from our research into other target populations, 
specifically the Spanish-speaking Hispanic population. Spanish-speaking Hispanics do not respond 
positively to messages, images or ads that single them out as a separate and unique minority 
population; however, LGBT do. They appreciate messages, images and ads that are crafted specifically 
with them in mind and that address their unique values and challenges as a community. 
Key takeaways about this audience include the following: 
Audience Insights 
Tobacco use 
Because Colorado’s LGBT community uses tobacco at much higher rates than heterosexuals, it’s 
important to understand more about this audience, their motivations to use tobacco and motivations to 
successfully quit in order to craft strategies and tactics to effectively reach them.  
 LGBT adults in Colorado are more than twice as likely as heterosexual adults in Colorado to 
smoke2 (38 percent of LGBT Coloradans use tobacco, compared to 18 percent of all Colorado 
adults.3)  
 Many LGBT say the reason that there is a disproportionately higher prevalence of smoking in the 
LGBT community because there is a social norm within the community that smoking is O.K.4    
 Nationally, 33 percent of LGBT people smoke—a rate 68 percent higher than the general U.S. 
population (compared to 19.5 percent of others).5 
 The LGBT community spends an astonishing $7.9 billion every year on tobacco, about 65 times 
the amount of money spent on all LGBT lobbying.6 
LGBT youth use tobacco at much higher rates than heterosexual youth, as well. They may also be at a 
greater risk because many of them start smoking at a younger age than heterosexual tobacco users. 
 In the U.S., 59 percent of LGBT youth use tobacco, compared to 35 percent of non-LGBT teens.7 
 “Ninety percent of smokers start in their teens, and LGBT smokers start even younger; in one 
survey, 13 years was the median age for girls.”8 
Despite these numbers, most LGBT do not perceive that smoking is a bigger health problem for them 
than for people in general.9 Therefore, it is important to change that perception and demonstrate how 
smoking significantly impacts the LGBT community.

Sample of Colorado Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, and Transgendered Smokers. Nicotine and Tobacco Research Advance Access: Published January 17, 
2012, 1-9. doi: 10.1093/ntr/ntr303 
3 See footnote 1 
4 See footnote 1 
5 NATS: Current Tobacco Use Among Adults in the United States: Findings From the National Adult Tobacco Survey Brian A. King, Shanta R. 
Dube, Michael A. Tynan American Journal of Public Health: November 2012, Vol. 102, No. 11, pp. e93-e100. 
6 See footnote 5  and http://www.lgbtfunders.org/resources/LGBTFundersTracking.htm  
7 See footnote 1 
8 Washington, Harriet A. “Burning Love: Big Tobacco Takes Aim at LGBT Youths.” Am J Public Health. 2002 July; 92(7): 1086–
1095...http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3222279/pdf/0921086.pdf   


--- PAGE 3 ---
3 
 
Motivations to use tobacco 
There are several factors that motivate LGBT adults to smoke. Some of these factors are similar to 
factors that motivate any adult smoker to use tobacco (e.g., part of a routine, a perceived stress 
reduction). However, because of certain influences unique to the LGBT community (as described below), 
some of these factors can have an even larger impact on LGBT tobacco users than they would on other 
tobacco users. 
Our examination of secondary research shows that there are several factors that are more pronounced 
in the LGBT community leading to higher rates of tobacco use.10 While many adult tobacco users say 
they use tobacco to relieve their stress, or when they drink and socialize, these themes seem to be even 
stronger motivators in the LGBT community. 
 LGBT say they have more social stress than other adults because of their sexual orientation: The 
pressures of stigma, prejudice, rejection, and homophobia often lead LGBT to take up smoking 
as a way to combat stress and connect with other LGBT, who are more likely to be smokers than 
heterosexuals (especially when they are coming out).11   
o Note: This was a theme that was very prevalent among LGBT adults, but not among 
LGBT youth in the focus groups in El Paso County. LGBT youth talked about the stress of 
being a teen, but did not mention their sexual orientation specifically. In the adult group, 
participants mentioned the acute stress that comes with being LGBT, which seems to be 
a major driver for tobacco use. LGBT adults said they feel like they “need” tobacco to get 
through the difficult times in their lives. 
o LGBT youth in El Paso County talked about the importance of connecting with other 
LGBT youth who are more likely to be smokers. They even said that there was a social 
pressure to smoke and that it is difficult to say "no" when they are offered tobacco when 
they first meeting other young people like them. This pressure seems to be even more of 
an issue among LGBT youth than among non-LGBT youth focus group participants. 
o Like most tobacco users, LGBT also associate tobacco use with socializing and drinking. 
Research shows that the bar or club culture is an important part of the LGBT culture and that 
LGBT have higher rates of alcohol and drug use than heterosexuals. Because tobacco is often 
associated with these activities that are common among LGBT, it is no surprise that LGBT often 
use tobacco more than heterosexuals, particularly when they are socializing and drinking.  
o Note: This was another common theme among both El Paso LGBT focus groups.   
o LGBT are more susceptible to smoking, substance abuse, and other risky health 
behaviors as a coping response to “minority stress.”12, 13  Similarly, studies show that 
consuming tobacco and alcohol together can increase the pleasure users experience 
from either product alone, explaining why tobacco users consistently mention alcohol 
use as a contributing factor to smoking.14 
                                                                                                                                                                                           
9 California Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, and Transgender Tobacco Use Survey - 2004 
10 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
11 Mental Health and Wellbeing and Alcohol, Tobacco and Other Drugs use in Queensland LGBT communities – A Community Needs Analysis 
12 Why the Gay and Transgender Population Experiences Higher Rates of Substance Use 
13 See footnote 2 
14 US Department of Health and Human Services “Alcohol Alert: Alcohol and Tobacco.” 


--- PAGE 4 ---
4 
 
While some motivations to use tobacco among LGBT are similar to motivations identified by other adult 
tobacco users (stress and socializing), there are some factors that are unique to this population: 
o Because many LGBT feel like they are living outside of society because of their sexual 
orientation, this feeling of rebellion can be a powerful motivator to use tobacco. Secondary 
research identified LGBT who talked about how they felt like they were already not part of 
the social norm and using tobacco is just another illustration of that.15   
o The tobacco industry markets to LGBT specifically to encourage them to use tobacco. 
Tobacco companies offer financial support to LGBT festivals, bars, media, and local 
organizations. In exchange, some gay bars are prohibited from allowing any anti-tobacco 
promotion onsite.16 
o Note: This fact an effective way to get LGBT adult tobacco users in the El Paso 
focus groups to think about quitting. Many participants responded that the LGBT 
community has already endured enough discrimination and targeting, that they 
shouldn’t put up with being targeted by the tobacco industry.  
 
Cessation 
Smoking is a large part of LGBT culture. It is part of the social norm and an integral part of their 
community identity. That may be one reason why LGBT use tobacco at higher rates and why LGBT are 
less likely to quit, typically because they don’t try, or don’t have successful quit attempts. According to 
research, few LGBT think about quitting. And, as noted above, few LGBT think that smoking is more of a 
problem for LGBT than it is for the heterosexual population. That means communities need to work to 
get LGBT to think about quitting, access cessation services, and engage in successful quit attempts. 
However, it will be more difficult to communicate with this audience and encourage them to change 
their behavior than with other adult tobacco users. 
o Only 30 percent of Colorado LGBT smokers said quitting is on their agenda, compared to 
40 percent of the average smoking population.17  
o In Colorado, 75 percent of LGBT have tried to quit compared to 80 percent of all 
adults.18 
o Despite the fact that LGBT are somewhat less likely to have made quit attempts, there is 
no difference between LGBT and heterosexual populations’ average number of quit 
attempts before successfully quitting.19  (About 7 to 9 quit attempts before successfully 
quitting.) 
                                                           
15 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
16 American Cancer Society “Tobacco and GLBT Community” 
17 See footnote 2 
18 See footnote 1 
19 See footnote 1 


--- PAGE 5 ---
5 
 
 LGBT smokers do not access cessation services (i.e. QuitLine or provider advice to quit).20 
Because of this, many organizations suggest that public health campaigns should focus on 
supporting motivations to quit and providing nonclinical access to evidence-based treatments.21 
o A large minority of LGBT smokers say they are unlikely to seek cessation assistance 
through clinical encounters and one quarter of LGBT smokers in Colorado say they are 
uncomfortable approaching their doctors for smoking cessation advice.22 
o Two-thirds to three-fourths of respondents said four features would increase the 
likelihood that they would use a quitline: proven effectiveness (74.9 percent), expert 
advice (70.8 percent), free nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) (68.5 percent), and 
confidentiality (63.0 percent).23 
 Similar to the general population, LGBT smokers claim they want to quit for health, social and 
financial reasons. Most believe they will try, but some also believe they are beyond quitting.24 
o Note: This is consistent with our El Paso focus group findings with LGBT smokers and 
consistent with the findings from the focus groups with the general population. 
 In terms of policy change that can impact LGBT cessation attempts, research shows that smoke-
free home policies may appeal to LGBT smokers who are not ready to quit, especially those who 
live with a nonsmoker. Voluntary smoke-free home policies increase the likelihood of future 
cessation attempts.25 Because of this, it may be effective for tobacco control advocates to 
consider promoting smoke-free home policies among Colorado’s LGBT tobacco users in efforts 
to begin to encourage them to quit. It may also be effective to consider campaigns that 
encourage LGBT to quit with their partners because many Colorado LGBT smokers surveyed live 
with another smoker (48 percent).26 
o Fewer LGBT have smoke free rules than heterosexuals and twice as many LGBT smoke in 
their homes than heterosexuals.   
 Smoke-free rules: 68 percent LGBT/ 86 percent of heterosexual households.27   
 Smoke-free vehicle rules: 59 percent LGBT/ 73 percent heterosexual adults.28 
 Smoking inside homes: 23 percent LGBT/ 11 percent heterosexual households.29   
                                                           
20 See footnote 1 
21 Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment: Tobacco Program Tobacco Prevention and Cessation for LGBT 
Communities 
22 See footnote 2 
23 See footnote 2 
24  A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
25 See footnote 2 
26 See footnote 2 
27 See footnote 1 
28 See footnote 1 
29 See footnote 1 


--- PAGE 6 ---
6 
 
Message Insights 
Because LGBT do not believe that smoking impacts them differently than it impacts heterosexual 
populations, it is important to use messages that highlight how it does impact them. As we have found 
in other research, the most effective messages give people information they did not know already. 
Informing LGBT tobacco users about how smoking impacts their community specifically can be 
compelling to get LGBT to think about quitting. Primary (focus groups) and secondary research also 
show that messages targeted at LGBT populations that address issues that matter to LGBT are more 
effective among this audience than they are among other targeted audiences (youth, Hispanic etc.).  In 
our focus groups, youth didn’t respond as strongly to messages that highlighted facts specifically about 
tobacco’s impact on kids, as LGBT did about messages that highlighted facts specifically about LGBT. 
 More than one third (37 percent) of LGBT believe that anti-smoking campaigns ignore the LGBT 
community.30 So, LGBT appreciate and respond well to ads designed specifically for the LGBT 
community.31 This includes ads that use messages that address the LGBT community and images 
that show LGBT couples. This does not include health scare messages or other themes that also 
didn’t resonate among the general population. 
 Messages that address the LGBT community and its values include: 
o The impacts of tobacco (referencing LGBT relevant statistics). Messages that 
emphasize that tobacco causes more deaths than AIDS, drugs, breast cancer, and gay 
bashing combined (or HIV, illegal drug use, alcohol use, motor vehicle injuries, suicides, 
and murders) are effective at causing LGBT to think about quitting smoking.32,33 
 Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. This message puts the 
impact of tobacco in a way that relates it to concepts that are relevant to LGBT 
populations (e.g., drug and alcohol use, hate crimes). This is a message that 
tested very well with other audiences (“Smoking kills more people than alcohol, 
AIDS, car accidents, illegal drugs, murders, and suicides combined”), although it 
has been slightly edited to address certain statistics for the LGBT community. 
That customization made this message very effective for LGBT audiences. 
 Note: References to HIV and AIDS are effective with older (older than age 50) 
LGBT tobacco users, but should not be used with younger LGBT tobacco users. 
o Tobacco industry manipulation. Messages that reveal how the tobacco industry 
manipulates LGBT to use tobacco are shown to be effective in encouraging LGBT to 
quit.34 Also, specific messages about financial contributions by the tobacco industry to 
anti-gay politicians may help in damaging the image of the tobacco industry and further 
a community-wide pressure against smoking.35  
                                                           
30 California Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, and Transgender Tobacco Use Survey - 2004 
31 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
32 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
33 See footnote 1  
34 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
35 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 


--- PAGE 7 ---
7 
 
 Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso LGBT adult focus groups. It seemed 
to really bother the LGBT participants that the tobacco companies target them – 
a "vulnerable" population, in their words. They said the LGBT community has 
“already faced enough challenges” and “overcome enough hurdles” that they 
shouldn’t also have to worry about being a target of the tobacco industry. While 
this was an important message point for LGBT adults, this did not resonate at all 
with LGBT youth. 
o Tobacco’s impact on the LGBT community. The anti-industry/anti-gay message uses 
social pressure among a close-knit group to position smoking as something that harms 
the whole LGBT community – not just the individual smoker. This can be particularly 
powerful for many in the LGBT community who say they are a vulnerable population 
and want to stop the discrimination, abuse and hate crime violence. Additionally, LGBT 
are more likely to feel part of a “community” than an adult in the general population. 
While low-SES and straight to work young adults responded to how their tobacco use 
would impact their families and people they care about, among LGBT, their circles seem 
much larger and they are moved by how their tobacco use impacts the people they care 
about and the larger LGBT community. 
 This message helps to counter the beliefs that “it won’t happen to me” that 
many smokers hold, including LGBT smokers.  
 It also serves to neutralize the feelings of fatalism (“Something’s going to get 
me anyway”) or rebellion (“Don’t tell me what to do – I’m already not part of 
the social norm”).36  
 Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups, especially 
among LGBT adults. While all adult tobacco users seem to share this 
same sense of fatalism, LGBT individuals are more likely to think of 
themselves as part of a community whose individual members need to 
take better care of themselves and take individual actions (e.g., living 
healthy lives) that will to make the LGBT community stronger overall. 
 Messages focused on vanity, immediate health impacts such as impotence, and long-term 
health effects are of interest but are not strong motivators to encourage LGBT to quit.37 This is 
also consistent with our research among the general population. 
o Note: The El Paso focus group findings support this. 
 Some secondary research shows that messages that talk about how tobacco weakens the 
immune system and speeds the progression of AIDS and is linked to health problems that are 
                                                           
36 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
37 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 


--- PAGE 8 ---
8 
 
unique to the HIV+ population is more relevant to the LGBT population.38 However, we would 
not recommend using this strategy.  
o Note: We did not find this to be an impactful message in the El Paso LGBT focus groups 
and we believe that this message could potentially turn off LGBT, particularly younger 
(younger than age 50) who have not been personally impacts by HIV or AIDS. In El Paso, 
this message resonated well with one participant who works a lot with HIV+ populations, 
but did not resonate with most of the LGBT participants, especially those who are 
younger and less likely to know someone who is HIV+.  
 
Tactics Insights 
 Include LGBT elements, such as photography, in all media campaigns, including an authentic 
representation of the diversity of LGBT people during campaign development and advertising 
message testing and utilize community groups for recruitment/outreach in testing.39  
o Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. There was a huge positive 
impact in showing images of LGBT couples and LGBT participants liked seeing ads that 
seemed to be created for them and for their lives. 
 Recognize that differences exist within the LGBT community, so messages and approaches 
should be developed and tailored as appropriate based on geography, culture, background, 
etc., as opposed to a one-size-fits-all approach to showing LGBT. 
 Make the negative impacts of tobacco use more salient by linking the issue with existing LGBT 
community priorities (e.g., combine messages about tobacco and civil rights, obesity, etc.) 40 
o Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. 
 Supplement traditional paid and earned media campaigns with social media tactics. Use LGBT 
media outlets and social media channels for earned, paid, and online media campaigns, which 
provide a concentrated, qualified LGBT audience and are highly trusted by LGBT people. Low-
cost social media advertising placement can also be a very effective method to reach this 
audience. LGBT are more active on social networks than heterosexuals. Aside from being more 
active on Facebook and Twitter, LGBT are also more likely to read blogs, and as a result, most 
likely to be receptive to social media marketing. Social media strategies can be particularly 
effective for rural and youth LGBT populations. That may mean developing social media 
campaigns to take advantage of viral marketing or creating and maintaining blogs. Earned media 
and social media can be an inexpensive way to effectively reach LGBT communities. 41 
                                                           
38 HRSA Guide for HIV/AIDS Clinical Care: Smoking Cessation 
39 MPOWERED: Best and Promising Practices for LGBT Tobacco Prevention and Control 
40 See footnote 39 
41 See footnote 39 


--- PAGE 9 ---
9 
 
Message Strategies 
Based on our interviews with CDPHE subject matter experts, a review of national resources and focus group 
findings, we recommend the following approach for messages. It’s important to note that while some audiences 
(Spanish-speaking Hispanics, youth) do not respond positively to messages that single them out as a separate 
community, LGBT did respond positively to messages, images and ads that speak to the LGBT individual  or 
community and their values. 
LGBT AUDIENCES 
Strategy Messages 
Highlight how the tobacco industry is 
targeting them as a vulnerable minority* 
The LGBT community is a primary target of the tobacco 
industry. Tobacco companies give money to LGBT festivals, 
bars, media and local organizations to encourage LGBT to 
smoke and ultimately increase their profits. 
Empower the LGBT community to stand up 
to tobacco executives and overcome their 
addiction, as they have with other 
challenges they have faced as LGBT (anti-
discrimination laws, marriage equality and 
other important issues) 
Together, the LGBT community has worked tirelessly to 
fight for equality. We can work together again to 
successfully stop the victimization by the tobacco industry 
and protect more LGBT from becoming addicted to 
tobacco. 
Communicate the serious negative health 
consequences of tobacco in a way that 
relates to things they understand 
Smoking kills more people than alcohol, (AIDS+), car 
accidents, illegal drugs, murders, breast cancer, hate crime 
violence and suicides combined. 
+Note: AIDS/ HIV references are only effective if targeting 
older (50+) LGBT 
Focus on how their addiction can impact 
the people they care about 
Tobacco addiction can hurt the people you care about. 
Your partner or family may have to pay for your care if you 
get sick. Tobacco can also kill you. If you die, you will not 
be there for your partner, friends and family. 
Focus on how their tobacco use impacts 
their finances 
Using tobacco is an expensive addiction. A pack a day habit 
can add up. Money you spend on tobacco is money you 
can’t spend on other important things. 
*Note: In the one focus group in El Paso County, LGBT youth did not respond well to this message; however, older 
LGBT adults responded strongly to this message, perhaps because they had experienced more serious harassment 
and discrimination in their pasts. Secondary research shows this to be an effective message. While providing 
valuable qualitative information, focus groups are not statistically valid. Therefore, we recommend using this 
message. 

--- PAGE 10 ---
10 
 
 
Creative Recommendations 
Based on the primary (focus groups) and secondary research outlined above, we believe many of the 
existing cessation campaigns can be adapted and “transcreated” for the LGBT audience. Based on the 
research findings, using LGBT couples in the photography, and using copy points that reference the LGBT 
community and speak to issues important to them will be an effective way to communicate with LGBT 
tobacco users and encourage them to think about quitting. 
Also based on the research findings, there are also opportunities to develop new campaigns for the 
LGBT audience. Some of these concepts would also work with other tobacco users (low-SES, STW YA, 
Hispanic) with photography and messages targeted to LGBT. Some concepts would be unique to the 
LGBT community. The ideas for new campaign concepts are listed below: 
New Campaigns 
 Research shows that LGBT respond positively to messages and images that speak specifically to 
them. We recommend concepting a campaign for Colorado’s LGBT population that highlights 
how the tobacco industry is targeting them as a vulnerable minority or that encourages the 
LGBT community to change the social norm that accepts tobacco use. 
 As with all tobacco users, breaking the cycle of stress continues to be a major challenge for 
LGBT. Creating a campaign with this theme can help people find alternatives, especially those 
who have already taken steps to quit. This would resonate with many audiences, including LGBT. 
 LGBT responded to the idea of quitting as a couple and reinforcing the support one person can 
give another. This is a concept that resonated with many audiences who participated in the 
statewide focus groups, including low-SES adults and straight-to- work young adults and we 
believe we should look into creating a campaign with this theme.

targeting them as a vulnerable minority*

industry. Tobacco companies give money to LGBT festivals, 
bars, media and local organizations to encourage LGBT to 
smoke and ultimately increase their profits.

to tobacco executives and overcome their 
addiction, as they have with other 
challenges they have faced as LGBT (anti-
discrimination laws, marriage equality and 
other important issues)

fight for equality. We can work together again to 
successfully stop the victimization by the tobacco industry 
and protect more LGBT from becoming addicted to 
tobacco. 
Communicate the serious negative health 
consequences of tobacco in a way that 
relates to things they understand 
Smoking kills more people than alcohol, (AIDS+), car 
accidents, illegal drugs, murders, breast cancer, hate crime 
violence and suicides combined.

older (50+) LGBT

the people they care about

Your partner or family may have to pay for your care if you 
get sick. Tobacco can also kill you. If you die, you will not 
be there for your partner, friends and family.

their finances

can’t spend on other important things.

Based on the primary (focus groups) and secondary research outlined above, we believe many of the 
existing cessation campaigns can be adapted and “transcreated” for the LGBT audience. Based on the 
research findings, using LGBT couples in the photography, and using copy points that reference the LGBT 
community and speak to issues important to them will be an effective way to communicate with LGBT 
tobacco users and encourage them to think about quitting.

LGBT audience. Some of these concepts would also work with other tobacco users (low-SES, STW YA, 
Hispanic) with photography and messages targeted to LGBT. Some concepts would be unique to the 
LGBT community. The ideas for new campaign concepts are listed below:

 Research shows that LGBT respond positively to messages and images that speak specifically to 
them. We recommend concepting a campaign for Colorado’s LGBT population that highlights 
how the tobacco industry is targeting them as a vulnerable minority or that encourages the 
LGBT community to change the social norm that accepts tobacco use. 
 As with all tobacco users, breaking the cycle of stress continues to be a major challenge for 
LGBT. Creating a campaign with this theme can help people find alternatives, especially those 
who have already taken steps to quit. This would resonate with many audiences, including LGBT. 
 LGBT responded to the idea of quitting as a couple and reinforcing the support one person can 
give another. This is a concept that resonated with many audiences who participated in the 
statewide focus groups, including low-SES adults and straight-to- work young adults and we 
believe we should look into creating a campaign with this theme.

13 See footnote 2 
14 US Department of Health and Human Services “Alcohol Alert: Alcohol and Tobacco.” 


--- PAGE 4 ---
4 
 
While some motivations to use tobacco among LGBT are similar to motivations identified by other adult 
tobacco users (stress and socializing), there are some factors that are unique to this population: 
o Because many LGBT feel like they are living outside of society because of their sexual 
orientation, this feeling of rebellion can be a powerful motivator to use tobacco. Secondary 
research identified LGBT who talked about how they felt like they were already not part of 
the social norm and using tobacco is just another illustration of that.15   
o The tobacco industry markets to LGBT specifically to encourage them to use tobacco. 
Tobacco companies offer financial support to LGBT festivals, bars, media, and local 
organizations. In exchange, some gay bars are prohibited from allowing any anti-tobacco 
promotion onsite.16 
o Note: This fact an effective way to get LGBT adult tobacco users in the El Paso 
focus groups to think about quitting. Many participants responded that the LGBT 
community has already endured enough discrimination and targeting, that they 
shouldn’t put up with being targeted by the tobacco industry.  
 
Cessation 
Smoking is a large part of LGBT culture. It is part of the social norm and an integral part of their 
community identity. That may be one reason why LGBT use tobacco at higher rates and why LGBT are 
less likely to quit, typically because they don’t try, or don’t have successful quit attempts. According to 
research, few LGBT think about quitting. And, as noted above, few LGBT think that smoking is more of a 
problem for LGBT than it is for the heterosexual population. That means communities need to work to 
get LGBT to think about quitting, access cessation services, and engage in successful quit attempts. 
However, it will be more difficult to communicate with this audience and encourage them to change 
their behavior than with other adult tobacco users. 
o Only 30 percent of Colorado LGBT smokers said quitting is on their agenda, compared to 
40 percent of the average smoking population.17  
o In Colorado, 75 percent of LGBT have tried to quit compared to 80 percent of all 
adults.18 
o Despite the fact that LGBT are somewhat less likely to have made quit attempts, there is 
no difference between LGBT and heterosexual populations’ average number of quit 
attempts before successfully quitting.19  (About 7 to 9 quit attempts before successfully 
quitting.) 
                                                           
15 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
16 American Cancer Society “Tobacco and GLBT Community” 
17 See footnote 2 
18 See footnote 1 
19 See footnote 1 


--- PAGE 5 ---
5 
 
 LGBT smokers do not access cessation services (i.e. QuitLine or provider advice to quit).20 
Because of this, many organizations suggest that public health campaigns should focus on 
supporting motivations to quit and providing nonclinical access to evidence-based treatments.21 
o A large minority of LGBT smokers say they are unlikely to seek cessation assistance 
through clinical encounters and one quarter of LGBT smokers in Colorado say they are 
uncomfortable approaching their doctors for smoking cessation advice.22 
o Two-thirds to three-fourths of respondents said four features would increase the 
likelihood that they would use a quitline: proven effectiveness (74.9 percent), expert 
advice (70.8 percent), free nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) (68.5 percent), and 
confidentiality (63.0 percent).23 
 Similar to the general population, LGBT smokers claim they want to quit for health, social and 
financial reasons. Most believe they will try, but some also believe they are beyond quitting.24 
o Note: This is consistent with our El Paso focus group findings with LGBT smokers and 
consistent with the findings from the focus groups with the general population. 
 In terms of policy change that can impact LGBT cessation attempts, research shows that smoke-
free home policies may appeal to LGBT smokers who are not ready to quit, especially those who 
live with a nonsmoker. Voluntary smoke-free home policies increase the likelihood of future 
cessation attempts.25 Because of this, it may be effective for tobacco control advocates to 
consider promoting smoke-free home policies among Colorado’s LGBT tobacco users in efforts 
to begin to encourage them to quit. It may also be effective to consider campaigns that 
encourage LGBT to quit with their partners because many Colorado LGBT smokers surveyed live 
with another smoker (48 percent).26 
o Fewer LGBT have smoke free rules than heterosexuals and twice as many LGBT smoke in 
their homes than heterosexuals.   
 Smoke-free rules: 68 percent LGBT/ 86 percent of heterosexual households.27   
 Smoke-free vehicle rules: 59 percent LGBT/ 73 percent heterosexual adults.28 
 Smoking inside homes: 23 percent LGBT/ 11 percent heterosexual households.29

21 Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment: Tobacco Program Tobacco Prevention and Cessation for LGBT 
Communities 
22 See footnote 2 
23 See footnote 2 
24  A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
25 See footnote 2 
26 See footnote 2 
27 See footnote 1

29 See footnote 1 


--- PAGE 6 ---
6 
 
Message Insights 
Because LGBT do not believe that smoking impacts them differently than it impacts heterosexual 
populations, it is important to use messages that highlight how it does impact them. As we have found 
in other research, the most effective messages give people information they did not know already. 
Informing LGBT tobacco users about how smoking impacts their community specifically can be 
compelling to get LGBT to think about quitting. Primary (focus groups) and secondary research also 
show that messages targeted at LGBT populations that address issues that matter to LGBT are more 
effective among this audience than they are among other targeted audiences (youth, Hispanic etc.).  In 
our focus groups, youth didn’t respond as strongly to messages that highlighted facts specifically about 
tobacco’s impact on kids, as LGBT did about messages that highlighted facts specifically about LGBT. 
 More than one third (37 percent) of LGBT believe that anti-smoking campaigns ignore the LGBT 
community.30 So, LGBT appreciate and respond well to ads designed specifically for the LGBT 
community.31 This includes ads that use messages that address the LGBT community and images 
that show LGBT couples. This does not include health scare messages or other themes that also 
didn’t resonate among the general population. 
 Messages that address the LGBT community and its values include: 
o The impacts of tobacco (referencing LGBT relevant statistics). Messages that 
emphasize that tobacco causes more deaths than AIDS, drugs, breast cancer, and gay 
bashing combined (or HIV, illegal drug use, alcohol use, motor vehicle injuries, suicides, 
and murders) are effective at causing LGBT to think about quitting smoking.32,33 
 Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. This message puts the 
impact of tobacco in a way that relates it to concepts that are relevant to LGBT 
populations (e.g., drug and alcohol use, hate crimes). This is a message that 
tested very well with other audiences (“Smoking kills more people than alcohol, 
AIDS, car accidents, illegal drugs, murders, and suicides combined”), although it 
has been slightly edited to address certain statistics for the LGBT community. 
That customization made this message very effective for LGBT audiences. 
 Note: References to HIV and AIDS are effective with older (older than age 50) 
LGBT tobacco users, but should not be used with younger LGBT tobacco users. 
o Tobacco industry manipulation. Messages that reveal how the tobacco industry 
manipulates LGBT to use tobacco are shown to be effective in encouraging LGBT to 
quit.34 Also, specific messages about financial contributions by the tobacco industry to 
anti-gay politicians may help in damaging the image of the tobacco industry and further 
a community-wide pressure against smoking.35

32 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market

34 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 
35 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market

7 
 
 Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso LGBT adult focus groups. It seemed 
to really bother the LGBT participants that the tobacco companies target them – 
a "vulnerable" population, in their words. They said the LGBT community has 
“already faced enough challenges” and “overcome enough hurdles” that they 
shouldn’t also have to worry about being a target of the tobacco industry. While 
this was an important message point for LGBT adults, this did not resonate at all 
with LGBT youth. 
o Tobacco’s impact on the LGBT community. The anti-industry/anti-gay message uses 
social pressure among a close-knit group to position smoking as something that harms 
the whole LGBT community – not just the individual smoker. This can be particularly 
powerful for many in the LGBT community who say they are a vulnerable population 
and want to stop the discrimination, abuse and hate crime violence. Additionally, LGBT 
are more likely to feel part of a “community” than an adult in the general population. 
While low-SES and straight to work young adults responded to how their tobacco use 
would impact their families and people they care about, among LGBT, their circles seem 
much larger and they are moved by how their tobacco use impacts the people they care 
about and the larger LGBT community. 
 This message helps to counter the beliefs that “it won’t happen to me” that 
many smokers hold, including LGBT smokers.  
 It also serves to neutralize the feelings of fatalism (“Something’s going to get 
me anyway”) or rebellion (“Don’t tell me what to do – I’m already not part of 
the social norm”).36

among LGBT adults. While all adult tobacco users seem to share this 
same sense of fatalism, LGBT individuals are more likely to think of 
themselves as part of a community whose individual members need to 
take better care of themselves and take individual actions (e.g., living 
healthy lives) that will to make the LGBT community stronger overall. 
 Messages focused on vanity, immediate health impacts such as impotence, and long-term 
health effects are of interest but are not strong motivators to encourage LGBT to quit.37 This is 
also consistent with our research among the general population. 
o Note: The El Paso focus group findings support this. 
 Some secondary research shows that messages that talk about how tobacco weakens the 
immune system and speeds the progression of AIDS and is linked to health problems that are

37 A Qualitative Investigation of Smokers and Non-Smokers in the LGBT Market 


--- PAGE 8 ---
8 
 
unique to the HIV+ population is more relevant to the LGBT population.38 However, we would 
not recommend using this strategy.  
o Note: We did not find this to be an impactful message in the El Paso LGBT focus groups 
and we believe that this message could potentially turn off LGBT, particularly younger 
(younger than age 50) who have not been personally impacts by HIV or AIDS. In El Paso, 
this message resonated well with one participant who works a lot with HIV+ populations, 
but did not resonate with most of the LGBT participants, especially those who are 
younger and less likely to know someone who is HIV+.  
 
Tactics Insights 
 Include LGBT elements, such as photography, in all media campaigns, including an authentic 
representation of the diversity of LGBT people during campaign development and advertising 
message testing and utilize community groups for recruitment/outreach in testing.39  
o Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. There was a huge positive 
impact in showing images of LGBT couples and LGBT participants liked seeing ads that 
seemed to be created for them and for their lives. 
 Recognize that differences exist within the LGBT community, so messages and approaches 
should be developed and tailored as appropriate based on geography, culture, background, 
etc., as opposed to a one-size-fits-all approach to showing LGBT. 
 Make the negative impacts of tobacco use more salient by linking the issue with existing LGBT 
community priorities (e.g., combine messages about tobacco and civil rights, obesity, etc.) 40 
o Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. 
 Supplement traditional paid and earned media campaigns with social media tactics. Use LGBT 
media outlets and social media channels for earned, paid, and online media campaigns, which 
provide a concentrated, qualified LGBT audience and are highly trusted by LGBT people. Low-
cost social media advertising placement can also be a very effective method to reach this 
audience. LGBT are more active on social networks than heterosexuals. Aside from being more 
active on Facebook and Twitter, LGBT are also more likely to read blogs, and as a result, most 
likely to be receptive to social media marketing. Social media strategies can be particularly 
effective for rural and youth LGBT populations. That may mean developing social media 
campaigns to take advantage of viral marketing or creating and maintaining blogs. Earned media 
and social media can be an inexpensive way to effectively reach LGBT communities. 41

Message Strategies 
Based on our interviews with CDPHE subject matter experts, a review of national resources and focus group 
findings, we recommend the following approach for messages. It’s important to note that while some audiences 
(Spanish-speaking Hispanics, youth) do not respond positively to messages that single them out as a separate 
community, LGBT did respond positively to messages, images and ads that speak to the LGBT individual  or 
community and their values. 
LGBT AUDIENCES 
Strategy Messages 
Highlight how the tobacco industry is 
targeting them as a vulnerable minority* 
The LGBT community is a primary target of the tobacco 
industry. Tobacco companies give money to LGBT festivals, 
bars, media and local organizations to encourage LGBT to 
smoke and ultimately increase their profits. 
Empower the LGBT community to stand up 
to tobacco executives and overcome their 
addiction, as they have with other 
challenges they have faced as LGBT (anti-
discrimination laws, marriage equality and 
other important issues) 
Together, the LGBT community has worked tirelessly to 
fight for equality. We can work together again to 
successfully stop the victimization by the tobacco industry 
and protect more LGBT from becoming addicted to 
tobacco. 
Communicate the serious negative health 
consequences of tobacco in a way that 
relates to things they understand 
Smoking kills more people than alcohol, (AIDS+), car 
accidents, illegal drugs, murders, breast cancer, hate crime 
violence and suicides combined. 
+Note: AIDS/ HIV references are only effective if targeting 
older (50+) LGBT 
Focus on how their addiction can impact 
the people they care about 
Tobacco addiction can hurt the people you care about. 
Your partner or family may have to pay for your care if you 
get sick. Tobacco can also kill you. If you die, you will not 
be there for your partner, friends and family. 
Focus on how their tobacco use impacts 
their finances 
Using tobacco is an expensive addiction. A pack a day habit 
can add up. Money you spend on tobacco is money you 
can’t spend on other important things. 
*Note: In the one focus group in El Paso County, LGBT youth did not respond well to this message; however, older 
LGBT adults responded strongly to this message, perhaps because they had experienced more serious harassment 
and discrimination in their pasts. Secondary research shows this to be an effective message. While providing 
valuable qualitative information, focus groups are not statistically valid. Therefore, we recommend using this 
message. 

--- PAGE 10 ---
10 
 
 
Creative Recommendations 
Based on the primary (focus groups) and secondary research outlined above, we believe many of the 
existing cessation campaigns can be adapted and “transcreated” for the LGBT audience. Based on the 
research findings, using LGBT couples in the photography, and using copy points that reference the LGBT 
community and speak to issues important to them will be an effective way to communicate with LGBT 
tobacco users and encourage them to think about quitting. 
Also based on the research findings, there are also opportunities to develop new campaigns for the 
LGBT audience. Some of these concepts would also work with other tobacco users (low-SES, STW YA, 
Hispanic) with photography and messages targeted to LGBT. Some concepts would be unique to the 
LGBT community. The ideas for new campaign concepts are listed below: 
New Campaigns 
 Research shows that LGBT respond positively to messages and images that speak specifically to 
them. We recommend concepting a campaign for Colorado’s LGBT population that highlights 
how the tobacco industry is targeting them as a vulnerable minority or that encourages the 
LGBT community to change the social norm that accepts tobacco use. 
 As with all tobacco users, breaking the cycle of stress continues to be a major challenge for 
LGBT. Creating a campaign with this theme can help people find alternatives, especially those 
who have already taken steps to quit. This would resonate with many audiences, including LGBT. 
 LGBT responded to the idea of quitting as a couple and reinforcing the support one person can 
give another. This is a concept that resonated with many audiences who participated in the 
statewide focus groups, including low-SES adults and straight-to- work young adults and we 
believe we should look into creating a campaign with this theme.

ME M O R A N D U M 
TO:   Allison Hastey, Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment 
FROM:   Susan Morrisey, Abigail Kesner, Allison Nipert, SE2 
RE:  Key findings for Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual and Transgender (LGBT) audiences 
DATE:   January 28, 2014  
 
In order to continue developing materials for targeted audiences, we have created a summary of our 
research into Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual and Transgender (LGBT) audiences. In understanding how to 
communicate with LGBT audiences we reviewed national research into trends, messages and 
communications strategies. We also conducted primary research in the form of two focus groups: one 
with LGBT adults and one with LGBT youth in El Paso County. While the focus groups help to provide 
some insights, the findings cannot be seen as reflective of an overall trend. All this research provides the 
background for the information listed below. Below we outline preliminary recommendations on 
messages and overall direction, and suggestions to customize existing campaigns or develop new 
campaigns for LGBT audiences.  
Purpose & Methodology 
The discovery phase of our project included a review of existing research related to tobacco use, 
cessation strategies, messages and communications tactics for tobacco cessation among LGBT 
audiences. For a separate project, we also conducted two focus groups with LGBT youth and adults in El 
Paso County. The limited findings from that primary research are also included in this memo. 
Key Findings:  Research on Key Audiences 
LGBT communities have one of highest smoking rates of all disproportionately affected populations.1 
Researchers nationwide have conducted studies to determine contributing factors to this trend and 
effective messages and tactics for addressing this issue. These studies consistently show that LGBT 
populations respond better to messages targeted specifically to them. The findings from the two focus 
groups with LGBT youth and adults in El Paso County support this finding. 
                                                           
1 Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment: Tobacco Program Tobacco Prevention and Cessation for LGBT 
Communities

2 
 
This is significantly different than the findings from our research into other target populations, 
specifically the Spanish-speaking Hispanic population. Spanish-speaking Hispanics do not respond 
positively to messages, images or ads that single them out as a separate and unique minority 
population; however, LGBT do. They appreciate messages, images and ads that are crafted specifically 
with them in mind and that address their unique values and challenges as a community. 
Key takeaways about this audience include the following: 
Audience Insights 
Tobacco use 
Because Colorado’s LGBT community uses tobacco at much higher rates than heterosexuals, it’s 
important to understand more about this audience, their motivations to use tobacco and motivations to 
successfully quit in order to craft strategies and tactics to effectively reach them.  
 LGBT adults in Colorado are more than twice as likely as heterosexual adults in Colorado to 
smoke2 (38 percent of LGBT Coloradans use tobacco, compared to 18 percent of all Colorado 
adults.3)  
 Many LGBT say the reason that there is a disproportionately higher prevalence of smoking in the 
LGBT community because there is a social norm within the community that smoking is O.K.4    
 Nationally, 33 percent of LGBT people smoke—a rate 68 percent higher than the general U.S. 
population (compared to 19.5 percent of others).5 
 The LGBT community spends an astonishing $7.9 billion every year on tobacco, about 65 times 
the amount of money spent on all LGBT lobbying.6 
LGBT youth use tobacco at much higher rates than heterosexual youth, as well. They may also be at a 
greater risk because many of them start smoking at a younger age than heterosexual tobacco users. 
 In the U.S., 59 percent of LGBT youth use tobacco, compared to 35 percent of non-LGBT teens.7 
 “Ninety percent of smokers start in their teens, and LGBT smokers start even younger; in one 
survey, 13 years was the median age for girls.”8 
Despite these numbers, most LGBT do not perceive that smoking is a bigger health problem for them 
than for people in general.9 Therefore, it is important to change that perception and demonstrate how 
smoking significantly impacts the LGBT community.

Motivations to use tobacco 
There are several factors that motivate LGBT adults to smoke. Some of these factors are similar to 
factors that motivate any adult smoker to use tobacco (e.g., part of a routine, a perceived stress 
reduction). However, because of certain influences unique to the LGBT community (as described below), 
some of these factors can have an even larger impact on LGBT tobacco users than they would on other 
tobacco users. 
Our examination of secondary research shows that there are several factors that are more pronounced 
in the LGBT community leading to higher rates of tobacco use.10 While many adult tobacco users say 
they use tobacco to relieve their stress, or when they drink and socialize, these themes seem to be even 
stronger motivators in the LGBT community. 
 LGBT say they have more social stress than other adults because of their sexual orientation: The 
pressures of stigma, prejudice, rejection, and homophobia often lead LGBT to take up smoking 
as a way to combat stress and connect with other LGBT, who are more likely to be smokers than 
heterosexuals (especially when they are coming out).11   
o Note: This was a theme that was very prevalent among LGBT adults, but not among 
LGBT youth in the focus groups in El Paso County. LGBT youth talked about the stress of 
being a teen, but did not mention their sexual orientation specifically. In the adult group, 
participants mentioned the acute stress that comes with being LGBT, which seems to be 
a major driver for tobacco use. LGBT adults said they feel like they “need” tobacco to get 
through the difficult times in their lives. 
o LGBT youth in El Paso County talked about the importance of connecting with other 
LGBT youth who are more likely to be smokers. They even said that there was a social 
pressure to smoke and that it is difficult to say "no" when they are offered tobacco when 
they first meeting other young people like them. This pressure seems to be even more of 
an issue among LGBT youth than among non-LGBT youth focus group participants. 
o Like most tobacco users, LGBT also associate tobacco use with socializing and drinking. 
Research shows that the bar or club culture is an important part of the LGBT culture and that 
LGBT have higher rates of alcohol and drug use than heterosexuals. Because tobacco is often 
associated with these activities that are common among LGBT, it is no surprise that LGBT often 
use tobacco more than heterosexuals, particularly when they are socializing and drinking.  
o Note: This was another common theme among both El Paso LGBT focus groups.   
o LGBT are more susceptible to smoking, substance abuse, and other risky health 
behaviors as a coping response to “minority stress.”12, 13  Similarly, studies show that 
consuming tobacco and alcohol together can increase the pleasure users experience 
from either product alone, explaining why tobacco users consistently mention alcohol 
use as a contributing factor to smoking.14

However, it will be more difficult to communicate with this audience and encourage them to change 
their behavior than with other adult tobacco users.

o A large minority of LGBT smokers say they are unlikely to seek cessation assistance

financial reasons. Most believe they will try, but some also believe they are beyond quitting.24 
o Note: This is consistent with our El Paso focus group findings with LGBT smokers and 
consistent with the findings from the focus groups with the general population. 
 In terms of policy change that can impact LGBT cessation attempts, research shows that smoke-
free home policies may appeal to LGBT smokers who are not ready to quit, especially those who 
live with a nonsmoker. Voluntary smoke-free home policies increase the likelihood of future 
cessation attempts.25 Because of this, it may be effective for tobacco control advocates to 
consider promoting smoke-free home policies among Colorado’s LGBT tobacco users in efforts 
to begin to encourage them to quit. It may also be effective to consider campaigns that 
encourage LGBT to quit with their partners because many Colorado LGBT smokers surveyed live 
with another smoker (48 percent).26 
o Fewer LGBT have smoke free rules than heterosexuals and twice as many LGBT smoke in 
their homes than heterosexuals.

 Smoking inside homes: 23 percent LGBT/ 11 percent heterosexual households.29

Message Insights 
Because LGBT do not believe that smoking impacts them differently than it impacts heterosexual 
populations, it is important to use messages that highlight how it does impact them. As we have found 
in other research, the most effective messages give people information they did not know already. 
Informing LGBT tobacco users about how smoking impacts their community specifically can be 
compelling to get LGBT to think about quitting. Primary (focus groups) and secondary research also 
show that messages targeted at LGBT populations that address issues that matter to LGBT are more 
effective among this audience than they are among other targeted audiences (youth, Hispanic etc.).  In 
our focus groups, youth didn’t respond as strongly to messages that highlighted facts specifically about 
tobacco’s impact on kids, as LGBT did about messages that highlighted facts specifically about LGBT. 
 More than one third (37 percent) of LGBT believe that anti-smoking campaigns ignore the LGBT 
community.30 So, LGBT appreciate and respond well to ads designed specifically for the LGBT 
community.31 This includes ads that use messages that address the LGBT community and images 
that show LGBT couples. This does not include health scare messages or other themes that also 
didn’t resonate among the general population. 
 Messages that address the LGBT community and its values include: 
o The impacts of tobacco (referencing LGBT relevant statistics). Messages that 
emphasize that tobacco causes more deaths than AIDS, drugs, breast cancer, and gay 
bashing combined (or HIV, illegal drug use, alcohol use, motor vehicle injuries, suicides, 
and murders) are effective at causing LGBT to think about quitting smoking.32,33 
 Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. This message puts the 
impact of tobacco in a way that relates it to concepts that are relevant to LGBT 
populations (e.g., drug and alcohol use, hate crimes). This is a message that 
tested very well with other audiences (“Smoking kills more people than alcohol, 
AIDS, car accidents, illegal drugs, murders, and suicides combined”), although it 
has been slightly edited to address certain statistics for the LGBT community. 
That customization made this message very effective for LGBT audiences. 
 Note: References to HIV and AIDS are effective with older (older than age 50) 
LGBT tobacco users, but should not be used with younger LGBT tobacco users. 
o Tobacco industry manipulation. Messages that reveal how the tobacco industry 
manipulates LGBT to use tobacco are shown to be effective in encouraging LGBT to 
quit.34 Also, specific messages about financial contributions by the tobacco industry to 
anti-gay politicians may help in damaging the image of the tobacco industry and further 
a community-wide pressure against smoking.35

o Tobacco’s impact on the LGBT community. The anti-industry/anti-gay message uses 
social pressure among a close-knit group to position smoking as something that harms 
the whole LGBT community – not just the individual smoker. This can be particularly 
powerful for many in the LGBT community who say they are a vulnerable population 
and want to stop the discrimination, abuse and hate crime violence. Additionally, LGBT 
are more likely to feel part of a “community” than an adult in the general population. 
While low-SES and straight to work young adults responded to how their tobacco use 
would impact their families and people they care about, among LGBT, their circles seem 
much larger and they are moved by how their tobacco use impacts the people they care 
about and the larger LGBT community. 
 This message helps to counter the beliefs that “it won’t happen to me” that

 It also serves to neutralize the feelings of fatalism (“Something’s going to get

Tactics Insights 
 Include LGBT elements, such as photography, in all media campaigns, including an authentic 
representation of the diversity of LGBT people during campaign development and advertising 
message testing and utilize community groups for recruitment/outreach in testing.39  
o Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. There was a huge positive 
impact in showing images of LGBT couples and LGBT participants liked seeing ads that 
seemed to be created for them and for their lives. 
 Recognize that differences exist within the LGBT community, so messages and approaches 
should be developed and tailored as appropriate based on geography, culture, background, 
etc., as opposed to a one-size-fits-all approach to showing LGBT. 
 Make the negative impacts of tobacco use more salient by linking the issue with existing LGBT 
community priorities (e.g., combine messages about tobacco and civil rights, obesity, etc.) 40 
o Note: We found this to be true in the El Paso focus groups. 
 Supplement traditional paid and earned media campaigns with social media tactics. Use LGBT 
media outlets and social media channels for earned, paid, and online media campaigns, which 
provide a concentrated, qualified LGBT audience and are highly trusted by LGBT people. Low-
cost social media advertising placement can also be a very effective method to reach this 
audience. LGBT are more active on social networks than heterosexuals. Aside from being more 
active on Facebook and Twitter, LGBT are also more likely to read blogs, and as a result, most 
likely to be receptive to social media marketing. Social media strategies can be particularly 
effective for rural and youth LGBT populations. That may mean developing social media 
campaigns to take advantage of viral marketing or creating and maintaining blogs. Earned media 
and social media can be an inexpensive way to effectively reach LGBT communities. 41

Message Strategies 
Based on our interviews with CDPHE subject matter experts, a review of national resources and focus group 
findings, we recommend the following approach for messages. It’s important to note that while some audiences 
(Spanish-speaking Hispanics, youth) do not respond positively to messages that single them out as a separate 
community, LGBT did respond positively to messages, images and ads that speak to the LGBT individual  or 
community and their values.

fight for equality. We can work together again to 
successfully stop the victimization by the tobacco industry 
and protect more LGBT from becoming addicted to

consequences of tobacco in a way that

10 
 
 
Creative Recommendations 
Based on the primary (focus groups) and secondary research outlined above, we believe many of the 
existing cessation campaigns can be adapted and “transcreated” for the LGBT audience. Based on the 
research findings, using LGBT couples in the photography, and using copy points that reference the LGBT 
community and speak to issues important to them will be an effective way to communicate with LGBT 
tobacco users and encourage them to think about quitting. 
Also based on the research findings, there are also opportunities to develop new campaigns for the 
LGBT audience. Some of these concepts would also work with other tobacco users (low-SES, STW YA, 
Hispanic) with photography and messages targeted to LGBT. Some concepts would be unique to the 
LGBT community. The ideas for new campaign concepts are listed below: 
New Campaigns 
 Research shows that LGBT respond positively to messages and images that speak specifically to 
them. We recommend concepting a campaign for Colorado’s LGBT population that highlights 
how the tobacco industry is targeting them as a vulnerable minority or that encourages the 
LGBT community to change the social norm that accepts tobacco use. 
 As with all tobacco users, breaking the cycle of stress continues to be a major challenge for 
LGBT. Creating a campaign with this theme can help people find alternatives, especially those 
who have already taken steps to quit. This would resonate with many audiences, including LGBT. 
 LGBT responded to the idea of quitting as a couple and reinforcing the support one person can 
give another. This is a concept that resonated with many audiences who participated in the 
statewide focus groups, including low-SES adults and straight-to- work young adults and we 
believe we should look into creating a campaign with this theme.
